newsitem.title: UK: United says British open sky demands obstructive.
newsitem.headline: United says British open sky demands obstructive.

text.p: United Airlines said on Thursday that British airline demands to be allowed to operate domestic U.S. routes were blocking the way to getting an Anglo-U.S. open skies aviation pact and should be dropped as being immaterial.

Speaking to an American Chamber of Commerce lunch chairman Gerald Greenwald said in terms of commercial value the demands really amounted to only "one percent of the business issue" and suggested that the demand was being made by Richard Branson's Virgin Atlantic only to prevent a deal being done.
"I think those who are saying that are saying we don't want a deal at all,'" Greenwald said.
Failure to agree an open skies pact would block the proposed alliance between Virgin's arch rival British Airways and American Airlines.
Virgin has been a vociferous opponent of the controversial BA-American pact, complaining that it would dominate the British transatlantic market with more than 60 percent of all flights.

Under the alliance, BA intends to coordinate its 244 flights a week from Britain to 22 U.S. destinations with all of American's 238 flights a week from seven U.S. airports to 12 European destinations.
BA and American argue their deal will lead to greater competition because it will only go ahead if Britain and the U.S. agree to establish an "open skies" free market.

But talks between government negotiators broke down last month. U.S. airlines want BA to give up some of its 38 percent share of runway slots at London's Heathrow airport to give them room to compete and to be allowed "fifth freedom" rights to fly from Britain to third countries.

On the British side, BA says it should not have to give up slots while Virgin wants British government negotiators to press for "cabotage" rights which would allow British airlines to fly domestic routes within the United States and to be allowed to own U.S. airlines.
U.S. law bans foreign airlines operating in the U.S. and limits foreign ownership of a U.S. airline to a 25 percent voting stake.
Virgin later denied it was simply trying to block an open skies deal to scupper the BA-American alliance.

"If a deal is done with the American prize being Heathrow and onward rights to Europe and the rest of the world, then the least the UK consumer can expect is to be able to have the opportunity to fly onwards with a British carrier in the U.S., just as U.S. consumers would expect to do the same in Europe," said a company spokesman.
If the rules are changed Virgin has vowed to start up services in the U.S.

But Greenwald said in reply to questions about Virgin's new plan that if Branson wanted to set up in the U.S. and fly domestic routes he should gain access by taking a 25 percent stake in a U.S. carrier which would also spread the risks.

"I don't see that is an issue," he said. "More power to him if he thinks he can swim with the sharks like Herb Kelleher (founder of pioneer low-cost carrier Southwest Airlines). That's a very tough market."

He said outright cabotage rights were unlikely to be granted by the U.S. government because U.S. airline workers were so opposed to seeing foreign airlines come into their home market, unless a pan-European aviation treaty was agreed with the U.S.

"The U.S. unions are crazed over the cabotage issue. It is a highly political issue. The only way I can see it being resolved is to have it (agreed) between the whole of Europe and the whole of the U.S."
Virgin's spokesman said: "We would expect them as a U.S. carrier not to want competition in their own market. To us it's a major issue. If cabotage is there we pledge to take it up."

Currently only BA, United American and Virgin can operate U.S. services out of Heathrow but United and Virgin both say Heathrow is so overcrowded they could not compete against BA and American without more runway slots.

"In terms of seat share the number one and number two airlines serving the United Kingdom are proposing to merge in a market that is already effectively closed to competition," Greenwald said in his speech on Thursday.
